title: Missourians Veto New Gerrymander, and Make It Trickier for GOP to Adopt Another
author: Daniel Nichanian
content:
Missourians rejected the GOP’s latest attempt to gerrymander their state on
Tuesday, siding instead with the organizers who collected hundreds of
thousands of signatures last winter to force a veto referendum.

That means Missouri will keep its current congressional map, adopted in 2021,
rather than switch to the map that Republicans passed in late 2025 at Trump’s
urging. The result is a relief for Kansas City voters as it preserves the
district anchored around the city that the GOP tried to tear apart.

And it’s a blow to Republicans’ nationwide push to use an unprecedented wave
of mid-decade redistricting for an edge in the U.S. House.

Missourians also easily reelected Justice Paul Wilson, who in September joined
the rest of the Missouri Supreme Court in blocking state officials from
implementing the new map before voters could weigh in on it. Republicans vowed
[revenge](https://www.kctv5.com/2026/09/10/missouri-lawmakers-threaten-state-
supreme-court-justices-drop-contempt-charge-or-face-impeachment/) against the
court but then did not mount a serious effort to oust Wilson, the only
Missouri justice who was [on the ballot this fall](https://boltsmag.org/your-
state-by-state-guide-to-the-2026-supreme-court-elections/#MO).

With nearly all ballots counted, 63 percent of voters chose to retain Wilson
in an up-or-down election.

The referendum against the gerrymander, meanwhile, succeeded by a wide margin,
with 62 percent of voters opting to block the GOP’s latest gerrymander. In
Jackson County, home to Kansas City, the veto referendum received 71 percent
of the vote.

Tuesday’s results also keep Republicans from gaining an early edge in the 2028
cycle. The GOP could try to gerrymander Missouri again next year, but it would
face major political and legal headwinds. They’d be likely to face another
veto referendum. Plus, voters on Tuesday approved a [separate constitutional
amendment](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-and-montana-measures-aim-to-protect-
direct-democracy/) that will restrict lawmakers from just ignoring a ballot
measure and doubling down after a people’s veto.

“Missourians are fed up with politicians trying to rig the rules in their
favor and take power from voters,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of
People Not Politicians, the organization that led the efforts to pass the veto
referendum, told _Bolts_. “It’s best when people get to pick our politicians,
and politicians don’t get to pick their voters.”

* * *

While the congressional map adopted in 2021 already favored Republicans, GOP
lawmakers redrew the state’s districts last year to gain a seat in the
midterms. They [split up Kansas City](https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-
and-government/2025-09-10/kansas-city-missouri-gerrymander-congress-map-
republicans-cleaver) and dismantled the seat held by Emmanuel Cleaver, a Black
Democrat, turning it into a GOP-leaning seat. They also shored up a district
in the St. Louis suburbs held by Republican Representative Ann Wagner to make
her less vulnerable to a Democratic wave.

Nimrod Chapel, president of the Missouri NAACP State Conference, says the
gerrymander was “a Republican attempt to enact plain Jim Crow politics by
limiting Black voices in Kansas City.” He compared it to [other
schemes](https://boltsmag.org/kansas-city-police-funding-referendum/) by
Missouri Republicans to crack down on local governments in Kansas City and St.
Louis, both cities that have a substantial Black population.

“This was just partisan politics, with an extra dose of racism,” Chapel told
_Bolts_.

But nothing turned out as the GOP planned. Missouri allows citizens to block a
new law from going into effect if they can collect enough petitions to put a
veto referendum on the ballot, and Democratic-aligned groups poured time and
money into that effort. Republicans mounted an extraordinary effort to derail
the process; led by Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, they denied that a veto
referendum could apply to redistricting and tried to run out the clock so they
could hold the midterms under their new map.

The Missouri Supreme Court rebuked them [in
September](https://missouriindependent.com/2026/09/03/missouri-supreme-court-
blocks-gerrymandered-congressional-map-orders-referendum-vote/). The justices
ruled unanimously that the veto referendum should be on the November ballot.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/26253769215394-2400x1600.jpg)Missouri Secretary of
State Denny Hoskins walks into the courtroom for his contempt hearing at the
Missouri Supreme Court in Jefferson City, Missouri., Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026.
(Liz Rymarev/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via AP, Pool)

They also held that Missouri must hold November’s congressional elections
using the old boundaries drawn in 2021. Republicans appealed and got some
[temporary reprieves](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-
courts/ca8/26-2797/26-2797-2026-09-21.html) in federal court, but the U.S.
Supreme Court repeatedly rebuked them.

As a result, Tuesday’s elections were held under the 2021 map, and Cleaver
easily won reelection in Missouri’s Fifth District, which remained anchored
around Kansas City. Plus, Democrat Fred Wellman ousted Wagner in the Second
District, one of dozens of flips Democrats secured in red-leaning territory on
their way to flipping the U.S. House of Representatives.

And voters jumped on their chance to weigh in on the 2025 map. The result
stands in stark contrast with referendums in [California in November
2025](https://boltsmag.org/five-ways-2025-elections-affect-voting-rules-and-
democracy/) and [Virginia in April
2026](https://www.vpm.org/elections/2026-04-22/virginia-congress-
redistricting-gerrymandering-april-21-results/), where voters approved
gerrymanders placed on the ballot by state Democrats.

To win those elections, California and Virginia Democrats spent millions to
make the case that their new maps were a response to Trump-led efforts to
gerrymander Missouri and other red states. But Missouri Republicans did not
mount any such effort to defend their map once the supreme court greenlit the
referendum.

St. Louis Public Radio [reported last week](https://www.stlpr.org/government-
politics-issues/2026-10-26/proposition-a-missouris-trump-backed-congressional-
map) that there was no state campaign committee devoted to supporting the
gerrymander. The group opposing the map, meanwhile, raised millions to defeat
it.

The result added to the wave of failure the GOP experienced on Tuesday in its
yearlong effort to use mid-decade redistricting to gain an edge in the U.S.
House. Of the 15 Democratic-held seats that Republicans redrew since 2025 to
make them more vulnerable, they appeared on track as of Wednesday morning to
only flip two, with a third going to a runoff.

Chapel said he was relieved to see Missourians from around the state rally to
defend Kansas City, telling _Bolts_ that the results “should demonstrate to
fat cat politicians that Missourians will live by their motto—the Show Me
State. When politicians started pushing around citizens telling them they
can’t pick their leaders, Missouri citizens showed them.”

* * *

Republicans could still attempt a new gerrymander next year in advance of the
2028 elections; the party retained its majorities in the state legislature on
Tuesday and Governor Mike Kehoe, a Republican, was not up for reelection.

But any such repeat would have a new obstacle to contend with. Besides vetoing
the GOP gerrymander, Missourians approved Amendment 6, a constitutional
amendment [that is meant to strengthen safeguards for direct
democracy](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-and-montana-measures-aim-to-protect-
direct-democracy/).

The measure affirms that Missourians have a fundamental right to citizen
initiatives, which will make it harder for future laws to restrict the
initiative process. It also restrains lawmakers from circumventing the results
of a ballot measure they dislike.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/25343564059330-1-2400x1800.jpg)Lucas Kirk, of
Sullivan, Missouri, stands with boxes of petition signatures he helped collect
and deliver on Tuesday, Dec. 9, 2025, to the secretary of state's office in
Jefferson City, calling for a referendum election on new congressional
districts approved by the state legislature. (AP Photo/David A. Lieb)

In particular, Amendment 6 imposes new rules for what lawmakers can do after a
successful veto referendum. It says that, when voters veto a law, the
legislature cannot pass legislation that is “similar in effect” unless 80
percent of lawmakers support this. Missouri Republicans don’t have such a
large majority—far from it.

Republicans could try to pass a new gerrymander with a regular majority and
say their new map is different enough from the old one, so the requirements of
Amendment 6 don’t apply. If they go down that route, it would be up to
Missouri courts to decide whether the two maps are “similar in effect,” says
Derek Clinger, a legal scholar at the University of Wisconsin Law School who
researches democracy in state constitutions.

“I’d expect any judges or state supreme court justices applying the ‘similar
in effect’ standard to be skeptical of any legislation that doesn’t pass the
smell test, but I'm not sure where they’d draw the line,” Clinger told
_Bolts_.

The fight would likely end up in front of the Missouri Supreme Court, which
showed impatience toward GOP officials this fall on how they handled
gerrymandering, effectively
[accusing](https://www.courts.mo.gov/file/SC/Opinion_SC101805.pdf) Hoskins of
operating in bad faith and threatening to hold him in contempt. And Wilson,
the justice just retained by voters, would be part of future deliberations; he
has rebuffed Missouri Republicans on [direct democracy
cases](https://missouriindependent.com/2024/09/20/missouri-supreme-court-
opinions-amendment-3-abortion/) beyond September’s showdown.

Regardless, opponents of gerrymandering are sure to have another tool at their
disposal to stop a future gerrymander—the one they just used to sink the 2025
map.

They could once again collect signatures to block a future law and force a
veto referendum. It would be a time-intensive and expensive endeavor, but one
they now have a clear template for.

Von Glahn told _Bolts_ that his organization, People Not Politicians, is ready
for another veto referendum should Missouri officials try to adopt a new
gerrymander.

“We’re not going anywhere,” he said. “If politicians try this again, the
result will be the same.”
